newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian rabbit virus said working in arid areas.
newsitem.headline: Australian rabbit virus said working in arid areas.

text.p: Rabbit numbers have dropped by more than 65 percent in dry areas of Australia after the release of the rabbit calicivirus disease, but results from wetter regions were more variable, Primary Industries Minister John Anderson said on Wednesday.
Anderson released results from the first eight months of data collected as part of the two-year national monitoring and surveillance programme at 10 intensive sites across Australia.

Six months after the virus was released at more than 400 sites across mainland Australia, the disease now affected virtually all areas of high rabbit density and most areas of medium to low rabbit density, he said.
At intensive sites in arid and semi-arid regions, rabbit numbers dropped by more than 65 percent following arrival of rabbit calicivirus disease, he said.
Data from one site was not collected before the disease appeared, but many dead rabbits and abandoned warrens were found at the site, he said.
Data from intensive sites was supported by results from 54 broadcacre sites where data was being collected on rabbit numbers and disease activity.
At 11 of 13 of such sites in arid/semi-arid areas, rabbit numbers also dropped by more than 65 percent, he said.
The results were being backed up by pastoralists who were reporting amazingly low rabbit numbers in central Australia, given the season and conditions, he said.
"Although it's still early days, the initial impact of rabbit calicivirus disease looks like good news for landholders in the vast arid and semi-arid areas," he said.
"These people have been battling grazing by wild rabbits and associated problems of soil erosion and land degradation to varying degrees for the past 100 years," he said.
Results from wetter sites were more variable than for arid sites and needed more time for effects to be gauged, he said.
At one of the wettest sites, Central Tablelands in New South Wales, no decline in rabbit numbers was recorded.
